target.title: Imagined speech can be decoded from low- and cross-frequency intracranial EEG features
target.version: Version of Record, Nature Communications, published 2022-01-10; first public as bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/2021.01.26.428315 (v1, 2021-01-26) under the title "Imagined speech can be decoded from low- and cross-frequency features in perceptual space"

read.pdf: Figs. 1–7 captions and in-text descriptions read; no main-text tables; Supplementary Tables 1–2 are cited but not included in text.txt

entries.text: Low-frequency power and cross-frequency dynamics carry information useful for imagined-speech decoding.
entries.condition: Authors' abstract-level interpretation of the pooled ECoG analyses across three studies.

entries.text: The claimed contribution is hypothesis-driven decoding across motor and perceptual representation spaces, using features beyond BHA.
entries.condition: Authors frame this as a broad feature-space and brain-coverage investigation, rather than automatized feature selection on a large dataset.
entries.quote: While we confirmed the advantage of BHA for overt speech decoding, imagined speech could equally well be decoded from low- and cross-frequency features along vocalic and phonetic (perceptual) spaces.

entries.text: BHA is strongest for overt speech, while lower-frequency power and local CFC provide comparable imagined-speech decoding performance.
entries.condition: Within the reported offline, participant-wise analyses; imagined-speech comparisons concern binary grouped-item decoding in studies 1 and 2.

entries.text: Imagined-speech decoding was better for phonetic and vocalic perceptual representations than for articulatory representation, supporting flexible abstraction.
entries.condition: Binary classification of grouped speech items in studies 1 and 2; participant–representation pairs evaluated separately.

entries.text: The authors caution that overt-trained BHA representations may not transfer to imagined speech.
entries.condition: The paper compares overt and imagined speech features but does not report a cross-condition trained-decoder transfer experiment as the principal evaluation.

entries.text: The best spatial and frequency features vary substantially across participants and tasks, so authors argue strategies will need individual adjustment.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation for future imagined-speech BCI design; no prospective clinical deployment test is reported.

entries.text: The authors do not exclude that significant CFC reflects other signal changes between baseline and speech, despite their precautions against spurious coupling.
entries.condition: Applies to phase-amplitude CFC interpretation; authors nevertheless argue that specific decoding indicates item-related information.

entries.condition: State-of-the-art characterization in the introduction; the article separately cites previous covert-speech BHA results as similar to its own BHA result.

entries.text: The manuscript reports participant-wise cross-validation but no held-out-subject or session-independent test; whether trials from the same recording session and word items appear in both train and test folds is not described in the paper.
entries.condition: Generalization beyond the same participant and recorded task is therefore not directly evaluated in the reported primary decoding protocol; released code confirms trial-level within-subject folds.

entries.text: No separate external validation cohort or independently collected validation set is described; feature selection is nested within the training folds and reported performance comes from cross-validation.
entries.condition: This records the absence of an external validation protocol, not a claim that nested training-fold feature selection was omitted.

entries.text: The manuscript does not report fold-local normalization for classifier inputs; its stated no-normalization choice concerns per-band power averaging, not all later classifier feature scaling.

entries.text: The imagined-speech labels are instructed stimulus identities rather than independently observed per-trial speech correctness; the manuscript notes that imagined speech lacks behavioral outputs.
entries.condition: Authors monitored for overt whispering or silent mouthing and asked participants after the experiment to confirm task compliance, but no independent imagined-word response is available as ground truth.

entries.text: The article does not describe a separate BCI calibration phase or online user–decoder co-adaptation during these evaluations.
entries.condition: Analyses are offline and use instructed, cued trials; online adaptation is discussed as future work.

entries.text: The authors concede the signal-to-noise ratio is low, binary classification is far from a real imagined-speech BCI, and the epilepsy cohort supplied few non-aligned trials.
entries.condition: Limits inference to an offline proof-of-concept; authors' expectation of better performance in chronic-purpose implants is prospective speculation.

entries.text: The participants were epilepsy patients with clinically driven electrode placement, not a cohort implanted specifically for speech restoration.
entries.condition: Thirteen participants across three sites; electrode placement followed clinical evaluation needs.

entries.text: The authors could not control for all residual silent mouthing, despite task instructions and online/offline monitoring.
entries.condition: Applies to imagined-speech recordings; experimenters monitored participants and audio/video recordings were reviewed.

entries.text: Poor electrode-coverage overlap between studies 1 and 2 prevents a strong conclusion about differences between imagining hearing and imagining speaking.

entries.text: The present data do not establish whether hearing versus reading is the better cue for imagined-speech decoding.

entries.text: The authors state that word-level decoding is probably not the optimal unit for an efficient imagined-speech BCI and that phoneme decoding faces combinatorial explosion.
entries.condition: Future-system discussion; the experiments use words and a small syllable set rather than continuous language output.

entries.text: The authors describe online subject–algorithm co-learning as likely to improve performance but difficult to envisage for short-duration epilepsy implants.
entries.condition: No online BCI or chronic-purpose implant was tested in this study.

questions.q: Do these results establish an imagined-speech BCI that reconstructs continuous speech?
questions.answer: No. The reported endpoint is offline binary classification of grouped items in participant-wise cross-validation, not continuous speech reconstruction; the authors explicitly say binary classification is far from a real imagined-speech BCI.

questions.q: Which neural features and representation spaces best support imagined-speech decoding in this study?
questions.answer: Lower-frequency power and local CFC support decoding; phonetic and vocalic perceptual groupings perform better than articulatory groupings. The highest reported CFC Fisher distances are for imagined low-beta/BHA coupling, with regional medians reported separately.

questions.q: Can overt-speech BHA decoders be assumed to transfer to imagined speech?
questions.answer: No. The authors caution against that transfer; BHA power was significant for only one imagined-speech participant–representation pair, compared with ten pairs for other power bands.

questions.q: What evaluation and reproducibility limits should accompany the headline accuracy?
questions.answer: The primary decoding evaluation is within-participant, trial-level cross-validation on eight participants and binary grouped labels, without an external or held-out-subject test. The code also reveals global pre-fold z-scoring for PAC/MI and a 200-versus-1,000 surrogate-count discrepancy for feature-distance analyses.

questions.q: Ikeda 2014 (covert vowels, ECoG): which bands were decoder inputs; any phase or coupling features; accuracies vs chance?
questions.answer: High-gamma 70-110 Hz power plus separate theta, alpha and beta power decoders; linear SVM, 15-fold CV, 3 classes; significant HG electrodes 42.2-46.7%, beta up to 55.6% in Broca area (chance 33.3%); no phase or coupling features.

questions.q: Pei 2011 (vowels and consonants, ECoG): which bands were decoder inputs for covert words; any phase or coupling features?
questions.answer: Spectral amplitudes at 8-12, 18-26 and 70-170 Hz plus LMP; Naive Bayes, ten-fold CV, 4 classes; covert vowels 37.5% and consonants 36.3% (chance 25%); no phase or coupling features.

questions.q: Denominators and multiple-comparison control for Fig. 7 binary decoding; CFC vs power comparison; how the paper characterises earlier covert decoders.
questions.answer: 8 participants x 3 representations (articulatory, phonetic, vocalic) = 24 pairs per family; thresholds per subject from an inverse binomial, no correction across pairs, bands or CFC combinations stated; no statistical test of CFC vs power and no combined decoder; the Discussion says earlier covert decoders used only BHA features.

questions.q: Leuthardt 2011: features and protocol for the imagined condition.
questions.answer: Imagined phoneme vs rest, 2 patients, online closed-loop cursor control; spectral power bins selected in a separate screening run (75-100 Hz; 40 Hz and 550-560 Hz); 73% and 69% (chance 46.2%); no phase or coupling features.

questions.q: Kunz 2025: was inner-speech decoding tested online on held-out material; WER and vocabulary?
questions.answer: Closed-loop evaluation blocks in the same sessions, evaluation sentences absent from training blocks, online retraining in T15/T16; 50-word WER 14-33% (3 participants), 125,000-word 26-54% (2 participants); intracortical spike features.

questions.q: Fig. 7 counts: distinct pairs or pair x band cells?
questions.answer: Preprint Fig. 7 (p. 12) plots one dot per participant x representation x band column, and above-chance counts are summed over band columns; the code tests 8 participants x 3 representations x 6 CFC combinations = 144 CFC tests. So 12 is a count of above-chance tests (inference from the figure layout and code).
